name: Shiraz
info: Shiraz is a city in Fars province in south-western Iran, mentioned in Elamite tablets of 2000 BCE, founded or restored in 693 under the Umayyads, and later a capital of the Saffarids, Buyids and Zands and a centre of Persian letters.

facts.founded: Shiraz was founded or restored in 693 by Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Thaqafi, brother of the Umayyad viceroy al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, or by the latter's kinsman Muhammad ibn Qasim; Elamite tablets of 2000 BCE name an earlier city called Tiraziš.
facts.where: On a plain at the foot of the Zagros Mountains, 1,500 metres above sea level, in the north-west of Fars province in south-western Iran, with a seasonal river, the Dry River, flowing through its northern part.
facts.known: The Elamite name Tiraziš; capital of the Saffarids and of the Buyids; Adud al-Dawla's library and hospital; the poets Saadi and Hafez; the philosopher Mulla Sadra; Karim Khan Zand's capital; the city where the Báb declared his mission in 1844
facts.today: Shiraz is the capital of Fars province and the fifth most populous city of Iran.

t: The name Shiraz appears on Elamite tablets dated to 2000 BCE, but the city was founded or restored in 693 by the Umayyads and stayed a provincial town until it became the capital of the Saffarids in the late 9th century.
Under the Buyids, who made it their capital, Shiraz became the largest city of Fars, and in the 13th century it became a leading centre of the arts and letters, the home of Saadi and Hafez.

Spared by the Mongols and by Tamerlane, Shiraz was sacked after a revolt against Nader Shah, rose again as the capital of Karim Khan Zand from 1762, and was lowered to a provincial capital under the Qajars.
dyk: Shiraz was spared by both Genghis Khan and Tamerlane: its local ruler offered tribute and submission to the first, and in 1382 Shah Shoja agreed to submit to the second.
ev: Elamite clay tablets name a city called Tiraziš, the earliest reference to Shiraz
Shiraz is founded or restored by an Umayyad governor
Amr, a Saffarid ruler, founds the city's first congregational mosque
The Buyids oust the Saffarids, and Adud al-Dawla later rules from Shiraz

The Báb first declares his mission in Shiraz
A pogrom in the Jewish quarter kills 12 Jews

sections.origins:
Shiraz stands in the north-west of Fars province in south-western Iran, on a green plain at the foot of the Zagros Mountains, 1,500 metres above sea level. A seasonal river called the Dry River flows through the northern part of the city. The earliest reference to the place is on Elamite clay tablets dated to 2000 BCE, found in June 1970 during digging for a brick kiln in the south-west corner of the city. They name a city called Tiraziš. Tablets from the Persepolis treasury archives, also in Elamite, mention major workshops in a place whose name is the ancient form of Shiraz, and the name appears on clay sealings found at the Sasanian ruin of Qasr-e Abu Nasr, east of the city.

There is no definitive record of the city before the late 7th century CE, but archaeological finds indicate that the site or its vicinity was settled as early as the 6th century BCE. Achaemenid and Sasanian remains lie around it, among them reliefs at Barm-e Delak and Guyim and Sasanian fortresses at Qasr-e Abu Nasr and Fahandezh. Scholars differ on what the ancient settlement was. Berney and Ring held that the lack of references in early Persian sources suggests no more than a way-station. Abdolmajed Arfaee pointed to its appearance in 84 tablets of the Persepolis Administrative Archives and to groups of workers as large as 490, and concluded that it was one of the most important settlements of the area.
sections.growth:
Shiraz was founded or restored in 693, after Arab armies had conquered Fars in expeditions from Basra between 640 and 653. The Sasanians held Istakhr, their capital in Fars, until the Arabs took it in 653. Because Istakhr was so closely tied to the Sasanian Empire and the Zoroastrian religion, the Arabs wanted a rival cultural and administrative centre nearby, and the new city was planned to be much larger than Isfahan. The ambition was not realised, and until at least the late 9th century Shiraz remained what John Limbert called a provincial backwater. As Fars gradually turned from Zoroastrianism to Islam and Istakhr declined, Shiraz became the practical centre of the province.

It grew most under the Buyids. Adud al-Dawla, who ruled Fars between 949 and 983, had a large library, a hospital and several mosques, bazaars, caravanserais, palaces and gardens built, and in 974 he built a fortified camp for his troops south of the city. One of his palaces stretched for nearly three miles and had 360 rooms. The city was divided into twelve quarters and had eight gates, and its prosperity came from the agricultural trade of Fars: grapes, linen, wool, cotton and rose and violet water. Benjamin of Tudela reported 10,000 Jews there in 1170. Its population was 60,000 in the 14th century and 200,000 in the 16th.
sections.rulers:
The Arab Muslim army captured the area around Shiraz in 641, and the city was founded or restored in 693 under the Umayyad Caliphate. As Abbasid authority weakened, regional dynasties arose. In the late 9th century the Saffarids under Ya'qub ibn al-Layth made Shiraz the capital of their autonomous state, which covered most of modern Iran. The Buyids under Imad al-Dawla Ali ibn Buya ousted the Saffarids in 933. His nephew Adud al-Dawla ruled Fars from 949 to 983 and in 977 added Iraq, the seat of the Abbasid Caliphate, to his domains, so that the Abbasids became a puppet state of the Shiraz-based dynasty.

The Mongols did not destroy the city, because its local ruler offered tribute and submission to Genghis Khan, and Tamerlane spared it in 1382 when Shah Shoja agreed to submit. In 1504 the forces of Ismail I, founder of the Safavid dynasty, captured Shiraz, which remained a provincial capital throughout the Safavid period. Emam Qoli Khan, governor of Fars under Abbas the Great, built palaces and ornate buildings in the style of Isfahan. Karim Khan Zand made Shiraz his capital in 1762. Agha Mohammad Khan, founder of the Qajar dynasty, destroyed its fortifications, and under the Qajars its governorship was a royal prerogative. In the Pahlavi era the tombs of Saadi and Hafez were constructed and presented to the public.
sections.life:
Under the Buyids two Zoroastrian fire temples still stood in Shiraz for the Persians who had not converted to Islam. The city had long had large Jewish and Christian communities. In the 20th century about 20,000 Jews lived there, most of whom emigrated to the United States and Israel in the latter half of the century, and the city also has a significant Baháʼí population. Most of the people are Persians and Shia Muslims. The crafts of Shiraz include inlaid mosaic work of triangular design, silverware, pile carpet-weaving and the weaving of kilims, and under the Buyids it was a market where rug weavers and painters sold their products.

In the 13th century Shiraz became a leading centre of the arts and letters, thanks to the encouragement of its ruler and the presence of Persian scholars and artists, and classical geographers named it Dar al-'Elm, the House of Knowledge. Saadi, the poet of the 12th and 13th centuries, was born there. After studying at the Nizamiyya of Baghdad he returned as an old man to a city that was, under the Atabak Abubakr Sa'd ibn Zangy (1231 to 1260), enjoying relative tranquillity, and he seems to have spent the rest of his life there. Hafez, the mystic Ruzbehan and the philosopher Mulla Sadra were also born in Shiraz, as was the 13th-century astronomer Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi. The Khan Theological School has tile-covered buildings dating from 1627. The city has a considerable number of gardens.
sections.crises:
After the fall of the Safavids, Shiraz declined. The raids of the Afghans made matters worse, and so did the rebellion of its governor against Nader Shah, who sent troops to suppress it. The city was besieged for many months and eventually sacked. When Nader Shah was murdered in 1747, most of its historical buildings had been damaged or ruined, and its population had fallen to 55,000 in the mid-18th century by one estimate and to 50,000 by another, the lower figure being a quarter of the population of the 16th century.

The city recovered under Karim Khan Zand, who employed more than 12,000 workers to build a royal district with a fortress, administrative buildings, a mosque and a covered bazaar, and who also built a moat and an irrigation and drainage system and rebuilt the walls. His heirs failed to hold what he had gained. Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar took his revenge on the city by destroying its fortifications, destroyed the Lak quarter that had been established in the Zand period and moved the national capital away from Shiraz.

In 1910 a pogrom began in the Jewish quarter after false rumours that Jews had ritually murdered a Muslim girl. In the riots 12 Jews were killed and about 50 injured, and the 6,000 Jews of Shiraz were robbed of all their possessions. In the 1930s the opening of the trans-Iranian railway shifted trade routes to the ports of Khuzestan, and much of the city's architectural inheritance, especially the Zand royal district, was neglected or destroyed under the Pahlavis.
sections.legacy:
Shiraz is remembered as the city of the poets Saadi and Hafez, whose tombs lie on the north side of the present city, and has been nicknamed the Athens of Iran. Other tombs include those of Khwaju Kermani, Shah Shoja and Karim Khan Zand. The Atigh Jame' Mosque, founded by the Saffarid Amr in 894, is the city's oldest mosque, and the Vakil Mosque and the Nasir al-Mulk mosque followed it. The Arg of Karim Khan, a citadel, stands beside the Vakil Bazaar and the Vakil Bath in the centre. The Qur'an Gate marks the entrance to the city.

Shiraz is also a holy city for Baháʼís. The Báb, Siyyid 'Ali-Muhammad, was born there in 1819, and on the evening of 22 May 1844 he first declared his mission there as the bearer of a new divine revelation, according to the Baháʼí account. His house became a place of pilgrimage and was destroyed in 1979. Another account says that on that evening he began discussions that led to his claiming to be an interpreter of the Qur'an.

Shiraz is the capital of Fars province and the fifth most populous city of Iran. Wine, gardens and nightingales have long been associated with it, and the city's Shirazi wine is said to originate there.

summary: Shiraz, in Fars province in south-western Iran, appears on Elamite tablets of 2000 BCE and was founded or restored in 693. It was the capital of the Saffarids, Buyids and Zands, and in the 13th century became a leading centre of the arts and letters, the home of Saadi and Hafez.
references: John Limbert, Shiraz in the Age of Hafez: The Glory of a Medieval Persian City (University of Washington Press, 2004)
notes: START: the articles say Shiraz was founded or restored in 693; I used 693 with circa false. The Elamite name Tiraziš (2000 BCE) is the earliest reference but the main article says there is no definitive record before the late 7th century CE and the site was likely settled by the 6th century BCE.

DISAGREEMENTS: (1) mid-18th-century population: 55,000 in the main article, 50,000 in the history article (the other sentence says it fell to 50,000 'one-quarter' of the 16th century in both); I gave both in crises, attributed. (2) The Qajar capital: Tehran in the main article, Sari in the history article; I wrote 'moved the national capital away from Shiraz' and named neither. (3) The Buyid dates: the main article says 933 to 949 to 983; the history article says Buyid 945 to 1055; I used the main article's 933 and 949 to 983 only. (4) The Báb: the main article says he declared his mission as the bearer of a new divine revelation; the history article says he began discussions leading to a claim to be an interpreter of the Qur'an; both given in legacy. (5) The Báb's house: the main article says it was destroyed in 1979 and paved over two years later as a public square; the history article says it was demolished and a mosque built; I wrote only that it was destroyed in 1979. (6) The history article says 'as early as the 11th century several hundred thousand people inhabited Shiraz', which sits oddly beside 60,000 in the 14th century; I left the 11th-century figure out.
The main article gives the Mongol and Tamerlane episodes without dates other than 1382; Genghis Khan's date is not given. 'Dyk' uses only that.

The 20th-century Jewish figure: the article says Shiraz 'also was home to a 20,000-strong Jewish community' without a year; I wrote 'in the 20th century', which follows from the emigration sentence; check. It also says 6,000 Jews in 1910 and 10,000 in 1170.
I wrote that Shiraz 'is said to' originate Shirazi wine; the article says 'Shirazi wine originates from the city'. The sherry claim and the modern liquor law were left out.

Left out as tourism, economy as of recent years, sport, transport, climate figures, twin towns, malls, the modern restoration projects, and notable living people. Planning of Adud al-Dawla's 'one of the congregational mosques ... has survived' left out. The etymology (sunlit plain) left out as a modern linguist's suggestion.

Extra statements I added from the article: Saadi's age and studies at Baghdad's Nizamiyya, and that he 'seems to have spent the rest of his life' there; Hafez's birth in Shiraz; Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi as 13th-century astronomer. The Khan Theological School (1627) is from the Higher education section.
